questions.stem: In tonight's revision the group works through a patch with slopes f_x = 2 and f_y = 3 over a 5 m^2 footprint. Find the area of the patch in square metres.
questions.explanation: The area element of a graph carries the factor sqrt(1 + 2^2 + 3^2) = sqrt(14), so the patch area is 5 sqrt(14) = 18.71 square metres. The 5 square metre footprint forgets the tilt.

options.misconception: confuses the tilted area with the projected disk area

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: Tangent vectors to a surface
questions.learningObjective: Explain how the two tangent vectors of a graph are built.
questions.stem: The group asks how the two tangent vectors of a graph are built. Explain it.

answer.exemplar: A graph z = f(x, y) has one tangent vector in each coordinate direction, written r_u = (1, 0, f_x) and r_v = (0, 1, f_y). The first moves in x while keeping y fixed, and the second moves in y while keeping x fixed, and each records how fast the surface rises as it goes. These two vectors span the small parallelogram that stands for one patch of the surface.

questions.explanation: The two tangent vectors of a graph run in the x and y directions with heights f_x and f_y, so they are (1, 0, f_x) and (0, 1, f_y). They span one small patch of the surface.
questions.hint: One vector per coordinate direction.

questions.stem: The group asks what the area element dS represents at a single point of a surface. Explain it.

answer.exemplar: At a point of the surface the area element is a tiny patch whose shape is set by the two tangent vectors there. Its size relative to the flat patch of the base plane directly beneath it is the stretch factor sqrt(1 + f_x^2 + f_y^2), so dS is that factor times dA. questions.explanation: The area element dS is the patch of surface at a point, and its ratio to the matching patch dA in the base plane is the stretch factor sqrt(1 + f_x^2 + f_y^2), which varies as the slopes vary.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: Surface area versus projected area
questions.learningObjective: Explain why surface area is never smaller than projection.
questions.stem: The group asks why a surface area can never fall below its projection. Explain.

answer.exemplar: Projecting a patch straight down onto the base plane shrinks it, because each tilted piece of the surface covers less ground than the piece directly beneath it. The shrink factor is the stretch factor sqrt(1 + f_x^2 + f_y^2), whose square root contains 1, so it is never below one. Only a flat patch, whose factor is exactly 1, has surface area equal to projected area.

questions.explanation: Projection shrinks every tilted piece of a patch, and the ratio of true to projected area is sqrt(1 + f_x^2 + f_y^2), at least one. Only a flat patch has surface area equal to its projection.
questions.hint: The stretch factor is never below one.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: Surface area versus projected area
questions.learningObjective: Reject a conclusion that a patch is smaller than its shadow.
questions.stem: A revision answer says a patch of surface area 50 m^2 projects onto 40 m^2 of base, and concludes the patch is smaller than its shadow. What is wrong?

options.text: Nothing is wrong, since the projection is always the larger area.
options.misconception: believes a projection can exceed the surface

options.text: The conclusion is right, because projecting a surface shrinks it in area.
options.misconception: confuses projection shrinking with area growing

options.text: The conclusion is wrong, because the two numbers should be equal for any patch.
options.misconception: believes surface and projected areas are always equal

options.text: The conclusion is wrong, because a tilted patch always covers more area than its projection.

questions.explanation: Projection shrinks a tilted patch, so the surface area is always at least the projected area, and 50 square metres against 40 fits that. The conclusion reverses the relationship.
questions.hint: Which of the two is always larger?

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: Area of a plane over a triangle
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the same recipe works over any region.
questions.stem: The group asks why the area of a plane over a triangle follows the same recipe as over any other region. Explain.

answer.exemplar: The area of a plane is obtained by integrating the area element over the region below it, and that integral is over the region itself. When the slopes of the plane are constant, the stretch factor sqrt(1 + f_x^2 + f_y^2) is the same at every point and comes out of the integral, so the area is the region area times one constant. The triangle shape matters only through its own area.

questions.explanation: The area of a plane is the integral of the area element over the region below, and for constant slopes the stretch factor comes out of that integral. What remains is the area of the region itself.
questions.hint: The region area times one constant factor.
